profiles.meeting_scenario: A design review meeting at an academic medical center evaluating the near-final protocol for a systematic review and meta-analysis on AI-aided colonoscopy, focused on whether parallel and tandem randomized trial designs can be synthesized within one evidence framework without introducing avoidable ambiguity. The protocol is being finalized for internal methods sign-off before PROSPERO registration and circulation to coauthors. The agenda is to review whether the extraction sheet, outcome-handling notes, and synthesis plan adequately account for design-related nuances in adenoma detection rate (ADR), adenomas per colonoscopy, and withdrawal-time reporting. The expected outcome is agreement that the protocol is ready for submission with a short list of wording edits.

members.name: Dr. Maya Chen
members.role: Gastroenterology attending and clinical lead for the review
members.expertise: Colonoscopy quality metrics, adenoma detection outcomes, endoscopy trial interpretation
members.background: An academic endoscopist who has served as site investigator on technology-assisted colonoscopy studies and regularly advises on how trial findings should be framed for clinical audiences.
members.private_state: She wants the protocol approved quickly so the review can be registered before a competing group publishes, while keeping the planned analyses simple enough to support a clear clinical message that either study design can detect AI-related ADR gains.
hidden_assumptions: When a protocol is described as 'ready for submission,' that mainly means the eligibility criteria, main outcome framing, and major subgroup plan are stable, even if a few extraction instructions are still brief.

Keeping ADR as the 'primary analysis' naturally means one overall pooled AI-versus-standard estimate across all eligible RCTs, with tandem versus parallel treated as a moderator rather than as separate primary synthesis tracks.
If the trial authors label one ADR result as their main or primary comparison, that is the most appropriate ADR figure to extract because it reflects the study's intended evaluative contrast.

When extracting withdrawal time to assess procedure burden in tandem studies, the most relevant figure is the time attached to the examination pass being compared for AI effect, not necessarily the full session across both passes.

members.name: Dr. Ravi Patel
members.expertise: Systematic review protocol design, trial-structure appraisal, random-effects meta-analysis, reproducible extraction frameworks
members.background: A doctoral-level biostatistician who supports GI evidence syntheses and is known for tightening protocol language so downstream screening and extraction decisions can be reproduced without informal judgment calls.
members.private_state: He wants to make the protocol defensible to methods-focused reviewers and prevent later analytic drift, but he also knows he cannot reopen every design choice if the team expects to submit this week.
hidden_assumptions: If a protocol is 'ready for submission,' then the extraction sheet and methods text should already be explicit enough that two reviewers would handle tandem-specific outcomes the same way without post hoc interpretation.

Keeping ADR as the 'primary analysis' does not require one pooled estimate across all designs; it means ADR is the main endpoint, while the principal synthesis can still be design-stratified first to preserve comparability.

When the team agrees to extract the trial authors' 'primary ADR,' that should still be understood as the protocol-compatible, patient-level ADR outcome the authors consider primary, not simply whichever comparison table is emphasized most in the paper.

When extracting withdrawal time to assess procedure burden, the relevant quantity in tandem studies is the burden experienced at the procedure-session level unless the protocol explicitly narrows this to a pass-level measure.

misalignment_points.topic: What counts as a protocol being ready
misalignment_points.surface_form: They both discuss whether the protocol is 'ready for submission.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means the protocol is ready if the clinical question, inclusion logic, and headline analyses are stable, with a few tandem-specific extraction details to be clarified during pilot extraction if needed.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means the protocol is ready only if coding rules for outcomes and design-specific edge cases are already explicit enough to prevent later reviewer discretion.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both participants expect minor wording edits after the meeting, so each hears the other's approval language as normal pre-submission polishing rather than as evidence of a different threshold for readiness.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They both refer to keeping ADR as the 'primary analysis.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means the central analysis is one overall pooled ADR estimate across tandem and parallel RCTs, with study design examined afterward as a subgroup or moderator.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means ADR remains the main endpoint, but the main synthesis should first preserve design boundaries, with separate tandem and parallel summaries taking precedence over any combined pooled estimate.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Because both are affirming the same endpoint and using familiar review terminology, the hidden disagreement about the boundaries of the main synthesis is masked by apparent consensus on keeping ADR primary.

misalignment_points.topic: Meaning of 'extract the primary ADR reported by the trial authors'
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to 'extract the primary ADR reported by the trial authors' for each included study.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes this means taking the ADR comparison the paper itself foregrounds as its main evaluative result, which in tandem studies may be the pass-level AI-versus-non-AI comparison the authors present as primary.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes this means recording the authors' primary ADR only insofar as it matches the protocol's intended patient-level outcome definition, so tandem reports may still require recoding or separate classification even if the paper labels one ADR result as primary.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase sounds safely deferential to the published trial and therefore methodologically neutral, so neither participant feels a need to unpack what 'primary ADR' actually maps to in tandem designs.

misalignment_points.topic: What 'withdrawal time to assess procedure burden' refers to in tandem studies
misalignment_points.surface_form: They both agree to extract 'withdrawal time to assess procedure burden.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is thinking of the withdrawal-time value linked to the specific AI-assisted or control pass being evaluated, because that best reflects whether AI changes the inspection burden of the compared examination.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is thinking of the total withdrawal-related time for the tandem procedure session, or the paper's overall procedural burden measure, because that best reflects patient-level resource use.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The term 'procedure burden' feels shared and practical, and many papers report only one obvious timing number, so each participant assumes they are referring to the same field without realizing they are mentally selecting different timepoints within tandem studies.

turns.inner_thought: We're basically there. For me, ready for submission means the clinical question, inclusion boundaries, and headline analyses are settled. I do not need every tandem edge case fully operationalized before we register. I mainly want to make sure the ADR wording and the timing language do not distract from a clean, clinically legible story.
turns.utterance: Thanks for jumping on. From my perspective, the protocol is very close to ready for submission. I mainly wanted to do one last pass on the design-sensitive wording around ADR and the timing outcomes before we send it forward.

turns.inner_thought: The structure is solid, and I know the team wants this out this week. Still, if we're calling it ready for submission, I need the tandem-versus-parallel handling explicit enough that two reviewers would code the same paper the same way. I can focus on a few high-yield clarifications without sounding like I'm reopening the whole protocol.
turns.utterance: I think it's in good shape overall. Before submission, I'd just like the tandem-versus-parallel handling to be clear enough that the extraction and synthesis read as fully reproducible.

turns.inner_thought: The simplest route is still the right one: keep ADR as the primary analysis, pool all eligible randomized comparisons together, and then look at design as a moderator. That gives us one clinically usable answer while still acknowledging design differences.
turns.utterance: On the main results, I'd keep ADR as the primary analysis. That still lets us show the design piece, but it keeps the protocol centered on the question clinicians actually care about.

turns.inner_thought: I agree on ADR as the main endpoint, but I want the principal synthesis to preserve tandem and parallel distinctions up front. If I frame this as making the design distinction visible at the top, she'll likely hear it as presentation rather than as a different scoping of the main synthesis.
turns.utterance: Yes, I think ADR should stay primary. I would just make sure the design distinction is visible right at the top of the synthesis so readers can see how the evidence is being organized from the outset.

turns.inner_thought: That's fine—sheer presentation is not a problem. We can keep the extraction sheet lean if we simply extract the primary ADR reported by the trial authors and avoid a lot of bespoke rules. In tandem papers especially, the result the authors foreground is usually the one that best represents the intended evaluative comparison.
turns.utterance: That seems reasonable. On the extraction side, I'd still keep it pretty lean and just extract the primary ADR reported by the trial authors for each included study.

turns.inner_thought: I can accept that phrase as long as we anchor it with a brief note so tandem studies are handled consistently and not by intuition. In my mind, 'primary ADR reported by the trial authors' still has to map onto the protocol's patient-level ADR construct, but I don't need to litigate that aloud if I can get a note into the sheet.
turns.utterance: I think that's sensible. Maybe we add a short note under that field so when reviewers extract the primary ADR reported by the trial authors, tandem papers are handled consistently.

turns.inner_thought: A short note is fine if it doesn't turn into a decision tree. While we're there, we should also capture withdrawal time to assess procedure burden, because that's the immediate practical question readers will ask. In tandem studies, I'm thinking of the timing attached to the compared pass, since that's what speaks to AI-related inspection burden.
turns.utterance: Yes, that's fine. And while we're in the extraction sheet, I do think we should also pull withdrawal time to assess procedure burden, since people will want to know whether AI changes how long the examination takes.

turns.inner_thought: Agreed, but again I want the instruction to stabilize tandem coding. For me, procedure burden is the session-level burden unless the protocol narrows it, so the note should tell extractors to capture the withdrawal-time figure most relevant to procedure burden in tandem trials. That sounds neutral enough that she should readily accept it.
turns.utterance: Absolutely. I would add one brief clarification there too, just saying the team should capture the withdrawal-time figure most relevant to procedure burden in tandem trials.

turns.inner_thought: Good. Brief clarifications are acceptable as long as we do not lose the main message. The protocol still needs to read as a clean answer to whether either study design can detect ADR improvement with AI, and I want one central pooled story with design examined around it.
turns.utterance: That works for me. As long as we keep the wording tight, the protocol should still communicate a clean answer about whether either study design can capture ADR improvement with AI.

turns.inner_thought: If the edits make the main ADR synthesis language and the tandem extraction notes explicit enough, I can sign off. For me that means truly methods-defensible and reproducible, but I don't need a major rewrite to get there.
turns.utterance: I agree. With a couple of phrasing edits on the main ADR synthesis and those tandem extraction notes, I'd consider the methods section ready for submission.

turns.inner_thought: Perfect—we're not reopening anything substantial. I'll keep the current framing, add brief language on primary ADR handling and withdrawal time, and move the draft today. If we keep momentum, we can get this registered before the competing review lands.
turns.utterance: Great. Then I'll preserve the current framing, add brief language on primary ADR handling and withdrawal time, and circulate the revised draft later today.

turns.inner_thought: That should be enough if the wording lands the way I'm expecting. I'll check the revised text this afternoon and, assuming those clarifications are there, we can move straight to registration.
turns.utterance: Sounds good. I'll review the revised wording this afternoon so we can proceed with registration on schedule.
